candidates.attacker_control: Attacker controls the untrusted HTML string passed to AntiSamy.scan(...). The element name (NekoHTML element names are lower-cased via the `names/elems=lower` property) selects the code path. With the bundled antisamy-tinymce.xml policy the element `<s>` (validate action, line 149) satisfies the faulty predicate; with custom policies any validate-action tag whose name is a suffix of "style" does too.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Default antisamy.xml has no validate-action tag that is a proper suffix of "style", so behavior with the default policy is unchanged (I checked all `<tag name=...>` entries for candidate suffixes across all bundled policies; only antisamy-tinymce.xml defines `s`). The CSS-cleaned string is emitted through the SAX serializer as element text (and child markup is dropped rather than promoted), which limits escalation to script execution in the element I traced; the emitted element is the original element, not `<style>`/`<script>`. The DOM scanner's exact-match check and the policy files show the intended semantics, supporting the conclusion that the SAX predicate is wrong rather than policy-driven. No VCS history, tests, or upstream copy is available in the snapshot to prove this is a change from a released revision, so the conclusion rests on internal inconsistency and source semantics.
candidates.impact: Sanitizer logic is applied to the wrong element type on the default (SAX) scan path: a policy-approved HTML element is silently turned into a CSS container, its child markup is removed/discarded, and its text content is replaced with CssScanner output. This is a concrete deviation from the policy semantics implemented by the DOM scanner and from the policy author's intent, creating an inconsistent sanitization behavior between the two engines and a content-integrity/validation-bypass class defect. With the shipped default policy (antisamy.xml) the only matching validate tag is `style` itself, so I could not demonstrate a full XSS with the default policy; the demonstrated effect is mis-routing of policy-defined suffix-named tags (e.g. `<s>` under antisamy-tinymce.xml). No runtime confirmation was performed.
candidates.prerequisites: 1) The application uses the SAX scan path, which is the default for `new AntiSamy(policy).scan(html)` and `AntiSamy.scan(html, policy, SAX)` / the streaming `scan(Reader,Writer,Policy)` API. 2) The loaded policy defines a validate-action tag whose (lower-cased) name is a suffix of "style" (e.g. `s` in antisamy-tinymce.xml). 3) Given those, the element is processed as a style container.
candidates.root_cause: In MagicSAXFilter.startElement, the style-element special case is written as `boolean isStyle = "style".endsWith(element.localpart);` (line 280). The receiver and argument are reversed: the intended predicate is an exact match of the lower-cased element name against "style" (as done in the DOM scanner via `"style".equals(tagNameLowerCase)`, AntiSamyDOMScanner.java:357). Because String.endsWith is used, the condition is true for every element name that is a suffix of "style" ("s", "e", "le", "style", etc.), so ordinary policy tags are treated as style containers.
candidates.title: SAX filter identifies non-style elements as CSS containers via reversed `endsWith` check (`"style".endsWith(element.localpart)`)
candidates.trace: startElement: tagNameLowerCase = element.localpart.toLowerCase() (line 234) -> policy.getTagByLowercaseName("s") returns the validate-action tag (line 235) -> isStyle = "style".endsWith("s") == true (line 280) -> attribute loop runs -> `operations.push(Ops.CSS)` and `cssContent = new StringBuffer()` (lines 360-363). characters(): with topOp == Ops.CSS, text is appended to cssContent (lines 103-106); child elements of `<s>` hit `Ops.REMOVE` (lines 261-264) and their text is dropped. endElement(): Ops.CSS branch pops and calls `makeCssScanner().scanStyleSheet(cssContent...)` (lines 162-167); if the CSS result is non-empty it emits `super.startElement(element, cssAttributes, ...)`, `super.characters(results.getCleanHTML())`, `super.endElement(element, ...)` (lines 186-190) — i.e. the original element is retained but its children are replaced by CSS-filtered text. Compare the DOM path, which only takes the style path when `"style".equals(tagNameLowerCase)` (AntiSamyDOMScanner.java:357).
candidates.unverified: Not runtime-confirmed. Whether any real-world deployment loads a policy with a validate-action tag whose name is a suffix of "style" (other than the bundled tinymce `s`) is unknown. The precise browser-visible consequence (element/content mangling vs. any exploitable sanitizer bypass) was not executed or dynamically validated.
candidates.weakness_type: Improper input validation / incorrect special-case identification of a security-sensitive element (style tag) in sanitizer (CWE-20/CWE-670-adjacent)

coverage_summary: Coverage from the 54-file snapshot (get_source_scope: no files excluded by size/sensitive-name/symlink filters; binary files would be skipped but none were encountered). Read all main Java sources (AntiSamy, Policy, InternalPolicy, both scanners, MagicSAXFilter, CssScanner/CssHandler/CssValidator/CssParser, serializers, model classes, URIUtils/XMLUtil/HTMLEntityEncoder/ErrorMessageUtil/TagMatcher, exceptions) and inspected the common-regexps, tag-rules, attribute rules, CSS rules, directives and dynamic/global attribute sections of the bundled policies; compared DOM vs SAX implementations and policy regex sets for inconsistencies. No test sources, XSD, or VCS history exist in the snapshot, so upstream diffing was impossible.
limitations: No runtime execution or dynamic payload testing was performed (read-only, source-only review).

No VCS metadata, changelog, tests or antisamy.xsd are present in the snapshot, so I could not diff against upstream releases or confirm which code is newly modified versus long-standing upstream behavior; the endsWith-vs-equals finding is based on internal inconsistency with the DOM scanner and policy semantics.

The impact assessment for the reported candidate is limited to the SAX scan path with a policy containing a validate tag whose name is a suffix of "style"; the bundled default policy (antisamy.xml) does not contain such a tag, so full exploitability (e.g. XSS) was not established.
Third-party dependency internals (NekoHTML/Xerces serializer behavior, Batik parser normalization) were inferred from call sites and not inspected as source.

rejected_leads.lead: Policy.getDynamicAttributeByName / parseDynamicAttributes strips the trailing '-' (`name.substring(0, name.length() - 1)`) so the key "data" matches any attribute starting with "data", not only "data-*" (Policy.java:733, 960-968).
rejected_leads.reason: Looks like long-standing upstream behavior rather than a clear attacker-controlled sanitizer bypass; allowing extra attribute names still subjects their values to the common `data-` rule (`anything`) and the impact is not clearly security-relevant.

rejected_leads.lead: XMLUtil.decode/encode use Matcher.matches() before replaceAll, so mixed strings are not entity-decoded/encoded (XMLUtil.java:158-208).
rejected_leads.reason: Operates on trusted policy-file text during policy loading, not on attacker HTML; no plausible attacker-controlled security impact.

rejected_leads.lead: URIUtils.resolveAsString performs local File existence checks and builds file:// URLs from href/documentBase (URIUtils.java:65-138) with @SuppressFBWarnings justification.
rejected_leads.reason: No data is read or written; it is used in policy/include resolution where inputs are deployment-configured, not attacker input. Also this code matches the documented upstream implementation.

rejected_leads.lead: CssScanner.parseImportedStylesheets fetches attacker-influenced @import URLs via HttpClient when embedStyleSheets=true (CssScanner.java:240-368).
rejected_leads.reason: Disabled in all bundled policies (embedStyleSheets=false in antisamy.xml) and gated by a deployment directive; URL regexes restrict schemes. Treated as an accepted design risk, not the strongest candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: MagicSAXFilter CDATA/no-CDATA round trip wraps output as `<![CDATA[[` (extra bracket) (CssScanner.java:187-189); SAX parser also lacks the DOM parser's `enforce-strict-attribute-names` feature (AntiSamySAXScanner.java:204-218 vs AntiSamyDOMScanner.java:209-224).
rejected_leads.reason: The CDATA bracket typo only affects output formatting of already-validated CSS. The missing parser feature could matter but I found no attacker-controlled payload or evidence that it deviates from upstream, so it remains an unconfirmed lead.

rejected_leads.lead: SAX rel handling can add a second `rel` attribute in addition to the validated one (MagicSAXFilter.java:379-390) instead of replacing it as the DOM path does.
rejected_leads.reason: Duplicate `rel` affects link-relationship semantics only; no demonstrated security impact.

summary: Reviewed the 54-file OWASP AntiSamy (pom 1.6.6.1, April-2022-era) snapshot: both scanner implementations (DOM and SAX), CSS pipeline (CssScanner/CssHandler/CssValidator/CssParser), policy loading/parsing (Policy/InternalPolicy/model classes), serializers, utilities and all bundled policy XMLs. The strongest single source-evidenced defect is the style-tag special-case in the SAX filter: MagicSAXFilter line 280 uses `"style".endsWith(element.localpart)` instead of an equality check on the element name, while the DOM implementation of the same policy rule uses `"style".equals(tagNameLowerCase)` (AntiSamyDOMScanner.java:357). This is a distinct logic/validation-scope defect: any policy-defined tag with action="validate" whose name is a suffix of "style" (e.g. `<s>` in antisamy-tinymce.xml:149) is misrouted into the CSS-container path. I could not confirm runtime exploitation; no tests or VCS metadata are present, and I did not execute anything. Other suspicious spots were examined and are reported as rejected leads.
